positions/word-of-faith-prosperity/name: Word of Faith and the prosperity gospel
positions/word-of-faith-prosperity/oneLi: Through Christ’s atonement believers are entitled to health and material blessing, which they appropriate by faith-filled confession and generous giving.
positions/word-of-faith-prosperity/coreC: Christ bore sickness and poverty as well as sin (Isa 53:4–5; 2 Cor 8:9), so healing and prosperity are covenant rights.
Words spoken in faith release spiritual power ("positive confession"); negative words can bind.
Giving is sowing a "seed" that God multiplies back (seed-faith).
God wills believers to prosper and be in health (3 John 2; Deut 8:18).
In stronger forms, believers are "little gods" restored to Adamic authority (contested within the movement).
positions/word-of-faith-prosperity/origi: E. W. Kenyon (1867–1948), influenced by Holiness, Higher Life and (critics argue) New Thought ideas, taught the authority of the believer and positive confession; Kenneth Hagin popularised Kenyon’s ideas (Rhema Bible Training Center, 1974). Oral Roberts’ "seed faith" (from 1950s), Kenneth Copeland, Fred Price, Benny Hinn and Creflo Dollar extended it through television. It spread worldwide: David Yonggi Cho’s "threefold blessing" (Korea), Edir Macedo’s Universal Church of the Kingdom of God (Brazil, 1977), David Oyedepo’s Living Faith Church Worldwide (Nigeria, 1981).
positions/word-of-faith-prosperity/stron: Scripture does promise material blessing to God’s people and presents God as generous (Deut 28; Mal 3:10; Phil 4:19), which much Western theology neglects.
Salvation in the Bible is holistic (shalom), including body and circumstances, which resonates with the poor in the Global South.
Sociologists (e.g. David Martin, Miller and Yamamori) note that it can foster sobriety, saving, education and entrepreneurship that lift families out of poverty.

Jesus and the apostles taught suffering, self-denial and contentment, warning against the love of money (Mark 8:34; 1 Tim 6:5–10; Phil 4:11–13); Paul himself was often poor and sick (2 Cor 11:27; Gal 4:13).
The Lausanne Cape Town Commitment (2010) and many Pentecostal scholars (Gordon Fee, 1985) reject it as a distortion of the gospel that exploits the poor and blames the sick for weak faith.

Critics such as D. R. McConnell (1988) trace Kenyon’s teaching to metaphysical New Thought rather than Pentecostal roots, and question its "little gods" anthropology and claims that Jesus was "born again" in hell.
High-profile scandals, luxury lifestyles and fundraising abuses have damaged its credibility.
positions/word-of-faith-prosperity/respo: Advocates reply that poverty is a curse Christ came to break, and that critics write from affluent contexts.
Many "soft prosperity" teachers repudiate extreme claims and stress generosity, stewardship and hope rather than guarantees.
Some Global South theologians argue for a "gospel of empowerment" that keeps prosperity’s holistic concern while rejecting manipulation.
positions/word-of-faith-prosperity/conse: Became one of the most widespread forms of popular Christianity in Africa, Latin America and parts of Asia, and in US megachurches.
Prompted vigorous critique from evangelicals, Pentecostal denominations, Catholic bishops and African theologians.
Influenced American political-religious culture (e.g. spiritual advisers to presidents) and media religion.
positions/imago-dei-substantive/name: Image of God as a capacity (substantive view)
positions/imago-dei-substantive/oneLine: The image of God is a quality or capacity in human nature — chiefly reason, will, freedom and the capacity for God — that distinguishes humans from animals.
positions/imago-dei-substantive/coreClai: Humans image God by their rational and spiritual nature.
The image (natural capacity) was damaged but not lost in the fall; the likeness (supernatural gift or virtue) was lost or obscured.
Augustine found a trinitarian image in memory, understanding and will.
This grounds the dignity of every human being.
positions/imago-dei-substantive/origin: Patristic (Irenaeus’ image/likeness distinction; Gregory of Nyssa; Augustine’s De Trinitate X-XV) and scholastic (Aquinas, ST I q.93); dominant in classical Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant theology.
positions/imago-dei-substantive/stronges: It explains what is distinctive about humans and grounds universal dignity in something every human possesses.
It has deep patristic and medieval support.
It made possible arguments such as Las Casas’ for the full humanity and rights of Indigenous Americans.
Critics note that Scripture never defines the image as reason, and that the view imports Greek philosophy.
If the image is a capacity, do infants, the severely disabled or people with dementia bear it less fully?
Historically the link between image and rationality was used to rank peoples and to describe women as less rational.
positions/imago-dei-substantive/response: Defenders answer that the capacity belongs to human nature as such, not to its exercise, so every human bears it fully.
Many now combine the substantive view with relational and functional emphases.
positions/imago-dei-substantive/conseque: Shaped natural-law ethics and human-rights language.
Underlies Catholic social teaching’s doctrine of human dignity.
positions/imago-dei-relational/name: Image of God as relationship (relational view)
positions/imago-dei-relational/oneLine: The image of God is not a property humans possess but the relationship in which they stand — to God, to one another (paradigmatically as male and female) and to creation — reflecting the relational life of the Trinity.
positions/imago-dei-relational/coreClaim: The image is constituted by God’s address and covenant, not by human capacities.
“Male and female he created them” (Genesis 1:27) shows that humanity images God in relationship.
Jesus Christ is the true image of God, and humans are renewed into it.
Personhood is relational, mirroring the Trinity.
positions/imago-dei-relational/origin: Anticipated by Luther’s view that the image is original righteousness in relation to God; developed in the 20th century by Karl Barth (Church Dogmatics III/1, 1945), Emil Brunner, Dietrich Bonhoeffer, John Zizioulas’ “being as communion” and in African “ubuntu” theology (Desmond Tutu).
positions/imago-dei-relational/strongest: It roots human identity in God’s love and in community rather than in abilities, so it includes those with limited capacities.
It fits the Trinitarian revival of the 20th century and Christ-centred readings of the image.
It resonates with African and Asian communal understandings of personhood.
Old Testament scholars argue that Barth’s male-female reading is not what Genesis 1 means by “image”.
Critics ask whether a relation can be “in” humans if it can be broken by sin.
Social-Trinitarian analogies may project human ideals onto God.
positions/imago-dei-relational/responses: Advocates respond that the relational view does not exclude capacities but grounds them in God’s prior relation to humanity.
They note that the New Testament itself defines the image Christologically, not as a list of faculties.
positions/imago-dei-relational/consequen: Influenced theologies of disability, marriage and community.
positions/imago-dei-functional/name: Image of God as royal vocation (functional view)
positions/imago-dei-functional/oneLine: To be made in God’s image is to be appointed as God’s representative and steward on earth, exercising dominion as his royal deputies — as ancient kings set up statues to represent their rule.
positions/imago-dei-functional/coreClaim: In the ancient Near East kings were called the “image” of a god; Genesis democratises this to all humanity.
The image is closely tied to the commission to “rule” and “subdue” (Genesis 1:26-28).
Humans represent God’s rule in creation; their vocation includes care for the earth.
Christ is the true human who exercises God’s rule perfectly.
positions/imago-dei-functional/origin: Developed by Old Testament scholars (Gerhard von Rad, Hans Wildberger; D. J. A. Clines, “The Image of God in Man”, 1968); expanded by J. Richard Middleton (The Liberating Image, 2005) and widely used in creation-care theology.
positions/imago-dei-functional/strongest: It best fits the immediate context of Genesis 1 and its ancient Near Eastern background.
It grounds environmental responsibility and the dignity of work.
It is democratising: every human, not just the king, represents God.
Critics note that dominion is a consequence or task of the image (“let them have dominion”), not its definition.
Ecological critics (Lynn White, 1967) argue “dominion” language encouraged exploitation of nature.
It may imply that those unable to exercise dominion bear the image less.
positions/imago-dei-functional/responses: Advocates stress that the royal image is modelled on God’s self-giving rule, including care, and that it belongs to the species and each member by calling, not performance.
They argue the functional view can be combined with relational aspects (a royal-priestly vocation in covenant).
positions/imago-dei-functional/consequen: Underpins evangelical and Catholic creation-care theology (e.g. Laudato Si’, 2015).
Shaped renewed theologies of vocation and work.
positions/holistic-dualism/oneLine: A human being is a unity of two distinct constituents, a material body and an immaterial rational soul, which can be separated at death and will be reunited in the resurrection.
positions/holistic-dualism/coreClaims/0: The soul is created by God and survives death in an intermediate state.
positions/holistic-dualism/coreClaims/1: Body and soul form one person; the soul is the “form” of the body (Catholic hylomorphism, Council of Vienne 1312).
positions/holistic-dualism/coreClaims/2: “Spirit” and “soul” in Scripture name the same immaterial aspect from different angles.
positions/holistic-dualism/coreClaims/3: Final salvation is embodied: resurrection of the body.
positions/holistic-dualism/origin: Held by most Fathers (with Platonic and Aristotelian inflections); defined in Catholic teaching at the Council of Vienne (1312) and Fifth Lateran (1513, immortality of the soul); confessed in Protestant standards (Westminster Confession 32.1).
positions/holistic-dualism/strongestArgu: It best accounts for biblical texts about an intermediate state between death and resurrection.
It preserves personal identity through death.
It has near-universal support in the historic churches.
positions/holistic-dualism/strongestObje: Christian physicalists argue that Hebrew anthropology is holistic and that the immortal soul is a Greek import.
Neuroscience links mental functions closely to the brain, making a separable soul seem less plausible to many.
Trichotomists argue it flattens the biblical distinction between soul and spirit.
positions/holistic-dualism/responses/0: Holistic dualists (Cooper) answer that Scripture’s holism concerns this life and is compatible with temporary separation at death.
positions/holistic-dualism/responses/1: They argue that neural dependence of mental functions in embodied life does not show the soul is reducible to the brain.
positions/holistic-dualism/consequences/: Shaped prayers for the dead, doctrine of purgatory and teaching on the intermediate state.
Grounds much Christian bioethics (ensoulment, end of life).
positions/trichotomy/oneLine: A human being has three distinct parts: a body, a soul (mind, emotions, will) and a spirit (the God-conscious faculty that is regenerated by the Holy Spirit).
positions/trichotomy/coreClaims/0: 1 Thessalonians 5:23 lists spirit, soul and body as distinct.
positions/trichotomy/coreClaims/1: Hebrews 4:12 speaks of dividing soul and spirit.
positions/trichotomy/coreClaims/2: The spirit is dead to God before regeneration and is made alive at new birth.
positions/trichotomy/coreClaims/3: Spiritual growth means the spirit ruling the soul and body.
positions/trichotomy/origin: Found in some Greek Fathers (Irenaeus, Origen, Apollinaris — whose Christology discredited it); revived by 19th-century German (Franz Delitzsch, 1855) and British writers, the Keswick and Brethren movements, and especially Watchman Nee’s The Spiritual Man (1927).
positions/trichotomy/strongestArguments/: It takes the explicit wording of 1 Thessalonians 5:23 and Hebrews 4:12 at face value.
It offers a practical map for discerning “soulish” versus “spiritual” life.
It explains regeneration as the quickening of a dead spirit.
positions/trichotomy/strongestObjections: Most theologians argue that soul and spirit are used interchangeably in Scripture (e.g. Luke 1:46-47; John 12:27 and 13:21).
Lists in Scripture (heart, soul, mind, strength, Mark 12:30) are not anatomies.
Apollinaris used trichotomy to deny Christ a human mind, and critics say it can foster anti-intellectualism or elitism.
positions/trichotomy/responses/0: Trichotomists answer that interchangeable usage in some texts does not cancel the distinction drawn in others.
positions/trichotomy/responses/1: They argue that their view, rightly held, safeguards rather than threatens the full humanity of Christ.
positions/trichotomy/consequences/0: Profoundly shaped Chinese house-church and Local Church spirituality.
positions/trichotomy/consequences/1: Underlies much Pentecostal and charismatic teaching on spiritual discernment.
